title: The truth will set you free (John 8:31–59)
carry: the truth shall make you free

cards: Some sentences escape their books. This one is carved in stone in the lobby of the CIA's original headquarters building in Virginia. It's on university buildings and library walls.

In Latin, it's the motto of Johns Hopkins University. Politicians quote it, journalists quote it, people who've never opened a Bible quote it. "And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free."
Out of context, it sounds like a slogan for information: get the facts and you'll be free. But in John it's the middle of a hard conversation, and the sentence before it changes everything.

teach.h: IF YE CONTINUE IN MY WORD.
teach.b: Here's the sentence before: "If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed." Continue means stay, abide, live there. So this truth isn't a fact you look up.

You come to know it by staying close to him, the way you only really know a friend after years together. And the freedom isn't political. His hearers object: "We be Abraham's seed, and were never in bondage to any man."
Jesus answers that whoever sins is a slave to sin.
The freedom he offers works from the inside out. The argument gets sharp, and both sides claim Abraham.
This chapter has hard words, spoken in a fierce argument among Jews, and over the centuries some Christians twisted those words into hatred of Jewish people, with terrible results.
Churches today, Catholic and Protestant, have taught clearly against that reading.
Then the line that ends the argument: "Before Abraham was, I am." Not before Abraham was, I was. I am.
The same two Greek words as the voice on the water, ego eimi. The tenses don't match, and his listeners hear a claim to God's own name. They pick up stones, and he slips away.

teach.h: THE TRUTH SHALL MAKE YOU FREE.
teach.b: This week: bread of life, Peter's to whom shall we go, judging rightly at the feast of booths, belly, a stone set down, light, and now truth that frees.

how: Christians read this passage as teaching that freedom comes from staying with Jesus's word; churches today also teach clearly against using John 8 to blame or demean Jewish people.

games.q: you've just said, "we were never in bondage to anyone." the argument has turned to Abraham. what does Jesus say last?
games.why: "before Abraham was, I am." his listeners hear a claim to God's own name and pick up stones; he slips away.

practice: Think of something true you've been avoiding saying: an apology you owe, a thank you never spoken, a boundary you need.

Notice how it sits in you unsaid, then imagine saying it simply and kindly to the person who needs to hear it, and notice what loosens. If you pray, ask for courage and gentleness; if you don't, choose the words you'd use.

wordCard.voice: Truth. Jesus's promise to those who continue in his word: knowing it by staying close, and being freed by it.

orig.note: Greek: truth. In John, truth is something you can know by staying close, not only a fact.
